title: Build the CSV export in isolation

scenario.brief:
Harbor's customers want to export dashboard data as CSV. The `insights-app` repository is shared by six engineers, and `main` deploys to production on every push, so nobody develops directly on it.

The team workflow: create a branch named after the feature, make small commits as you go, and only merge once the work is reviewed. Your branch for this work is `feature/csv-export`.

- Create the branch from `main` and switch to it.
- Add a new module `src/export/csv.js` that turns an array of row objects into CSV text (a header row from the object keys, then one line per row). Commit it.
- Wire it into `src/index.js` so the module is exported alongside the existing helpers, and commit that separately.

`main` must stay exactly where it is until the review is done. When you finish, your working tree should be clean.
scenario.whyItMatters: Branches are cheap pointers, and that cheapness is what makes safe collaboration possible. Working in isolation means your half-finished export can never break production, and reviewers can see the whole change as a unit.

files.README.md:
# Insights App

Dashboards for Harbor Analytics customers.

`main` deploys to production automatically. Develop on feature branches.

## Branch naming

`feature/<short-name>`, `fix/<short-name>`, `chore/<short-name>`.

objectives.title: Create feature/csv-export from main and switch to it
hints: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit. Creating one from main starts it at the same commit main is on.
`git switch -c <name>` creates a branch at the current commit and moves HEAD to it in one step. `git branch` lists branches and marks the current one.

objectives.title: Commit src/export/csv.js on the feature branch
hints: New directories do not need special handling; create the file and stage it.
Create the file (for example with `code src/export/csv.js` or `echo` redirection), then `git add` and `git commit` on the branch.

objectives.title: Wire the export into src/index.js in a second commit on the branch
hints: Each step of the feature is its own commit; the branch collects them.
Edit src/index.js so it requires './export/csv' and exports toCsv, then stage and commit.
Run `code src/index.js`, add the require and export, then `git commit -am "Export toCsv from package entry point"`

objectives.title: Leave main exactly where it was
hints: Commits go to whatever branch HEAD points at. If main moved, you committed while on main.
`git log --oneline --all --graph` shows where each branch points. main should still be at the "Add contributing notes" commit.

If main moved by mistake: `git branch -f feature/csv-export main` is not what you want; instead `git switch main && git reset --hard <original commit>` after making sure the commits exist on your feature branch.

objectives.title: Finish with a clean working tree
hints: Nothing should be left unstaged or untracked.
`git status` tells you what is pending.
Stage and commit remaining work, or discard scratch files with `rm`.

debrief.summary: You developed a feature on an isolated branch with two focused commits while production (main) stayed untouched.
internals: `git switch -c` wrote a new file `.git/refs/heads/feature/csv-export` containing the same commit hash as main, and changed `.git/HEAD` to point at that ref.
Each commit created a new commit object whose parent was the branch tip, then moved only the ref HEAD pointed at. main never changed because HEAD was not pointing at it.
In the graph, the branch is a chain of two commits growing from the commit main still points to.

keyCommands.note: Create and switch. `git checkout -b` is the older equivalent.
List local branches; `*` marks the current one.
See every branch and where it points.
Stage all tracked modifications and commit. Does not add new files.

commonMistakes: Committing on main because you forgot to switch; the deploy pipeline would have shipped unfinished code.
Using `git commit -a` and assuming it added the new module. `-a` only stages files Git already tracks.
Naming branches vaguely (`fix`, `test`, `tomasz-branch`). The team convention exists so branches are searchable.
debrief.atWork: Almost every team uses some form of branch-based development with protected main branches. Being fluent at creating, switching and inspecting branches is table stakes; the next labs cover how those branches come back together.
debrief.interview: "What is a branch in Git, physically?" The answer is a 41-byte file containing a commit hash. Explaining why that makes branching instant tends to impress.

solution: git commit -am "Export toCsv from package entry point"
